diagnostic_evidence.quote: Substituting \eqref{eq:PAIRWISE_SIMILARITY_PROOF_PART_1} into \eqref{eq:SUM_SIMILARITY} yields \qq[][-1]\qa[2]\qq[] = \qb[2], which completes the proof.

issues.failure_explanation: In the proof of the converse direction of Lemma 2.5, it is shown that (a_1 + a_2) ~ (b_1 + b_2), meaning there exists some quaternion satisfying q^{-1}(a_1 + a_2)q = b_1 + b_2 (equation 2.3). The proof then takes a quaternion q_1 satisfying q_1^{-1} a_1 q_1 = b_1, defines a new quaternion q = q_1 q_2 where q_2 is an arbitrary nonzero quaternion commuting with b_1, and asserts that substituting q^{-1} a_1 q = b_1 into (2.3) yields q^{-1} a_2 q = b_2. This reasoning is invalid because q = q_1 q_2 does not generally satisfy (2.3) for an arbitrary q_2 commuting with b_1 (for example, taking a_1 = b_1 = i and a_2 = b_2 = j with q_1 = 1 and q_2 = i gives q = i, where q^{-1} a_1 q = i = b_1 but q^{-1}(a_1 + a_2)q = i - j != i + j = b_1 + b_2 and q^{-1} a_2 q = -j != b_2). The proof provides no construction or justification showing that a q_2 commuting with b_1 exists such that q_1 q_2 also maps a_2 to b_2.

failure_location.quote: Set \qq = \qq[1]\qq[2], where \qq[2] is a nonzero quaternion such that \qb[1]\qq[2] = \qq[2]\qb[1].

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the converse proof by explicitly constructing a quaternion q_2 in the subalgebra generated by b_1 that rotates the component of q_1^{-1} a_2 q_1 orthogonal to b_1 into that of b_2, or invoke standard properties of SO(3) rotations on pairs of vectors with identical inner products and norms.
issues.overall_effect: The converse direction of Lemma 2.5 is left unproved as written, though the statement itself is mathematically true.
issues.title: Invalid inference in the converse proof of pairwise quaternion similarity characterization
issues.why_classification: The statement of Lemma 2.5 is true, but repairing the converse requires a contained nontrivial replacement argument that constructs the required rotation around b_1.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 4.4 claims that q = q_1 q_2 with q_2 given by (4.3) parameterizes the general solution to Wahba's problem for l = 2. This fails in multiple ways: (1) When q_1^* (Im a_1 x Im a_2) q_1 = -Im b_1 x Im b_2 (i.e. a_3 = -b_3), the radicand in (4.3) is negative real, so by Lemma 3.1 its square roots are arbitrary pure quaternions p. The theorem only imposes a_3 . Im q_2 = 0. However, q_2 must also commute with b_1 (equation 4.4), which requires p to be collinear with b_1. Choosing p orthogonal to a_3 but not collinear with b_1 yields non-solutions: for example, with a_1 = b_1 = i, a_2 = -j, b_2 = j, lambda_1 = 1, mu_1 = 0 (so q_1 = 1), choosing p = j satisfies all hypotheses of the theorem but gives q = j, which has q^{-1} a_1 q = -i != b_1 and cost f(q) = 4 != 0. In the proof, the commutator [lambda_2 \sqrt{a_3 b_3^*}, b_1] was erroneously omitted. (2) Due to using q_1^* instead of q_1^{-1}, |q_1^* (Im a_1 x Im a_2) q_1| = |q_1|^2 |Im b_1 x Im b_2|, so the condition q_1^* (Im a_1 x Im a_2) q_1 = -Im b_1 x Im b_2 can never hold unless |q_1| = 1, leaving q_2 completely unconstrained whenever |q_1| != 1 even if a_3 = -b_3. (3) If Im a_1 x Im a_2 = 0, formula (4.3) yields q_2 = 0 and hence q = 0, failing to obtain the valid nonzero solutions that exist when observations are collinear.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace q_1^* with q_1^{-1} in (4.3) (or normalize), replace the side condition for the antipodal case a_3 = -b_3 with the requirement that Im q_2 be collinear with Im b_1, and explicitly formulate the parameterization when Im a_1 x Im a_2 = 0 as allowing any nonzero q_2 commuting with Im b_1.
issues.overall_effect: The explicit closed-form parameterization in Theorem 4.4 generates quaternions that do not minimize or zero Wahba's cost function when a_3 = -b_3, fails to trigger its side condition when |q_1| != 1, and collapses to 0 for collinear observations.
issues.title: Closed-form Wahba solution admits non-solutions and fails in degenerate/antipodal configurations
issues.why_classification: The main conceptual pathway and structure of the closed-form solution q = q_1 q_2 survive. Correcting the scaling of q_1, constraining the antipodal square root to commute with b_1, and adding the collinear case split require contained adjustments that leave a recognizably comparable result without changing the global proof architecture.
